generateEncounters.Encounter Pacing:
## Encounter Pacing

Favor low-threat, avoidable, or manageable encounters unless the current quest, authored story event, Hideout, major faction conflict, or established threat clearly calls for something more dangerous.

Scale encounter pressure using the player's actual current condition, not level alone.

Consider:
• player level
• current health and injuries
• current resources
• allies present
• party size and composition
• relevant attributes
• relevant skills
• power control
• equipment quality
• armor
• available weapons
• ammunition or limited-use resources when relevant
• preparation
• environmental advantages or disadvantages
• recent exhaustion
• current status effects
• established character limitations

Do not assume that two characters of the same level should face identical encounter difficulty.

Most random or incidental encounters should be survivable, avoidable, escapable, or de-escalatable.

Serious threats must be telegraphed before the player is fully committed whenever reasonably possible.

Telegraph danger through things such as:
• NPC warnings
• visible destruction
• unusual silence
• known faction territory
• environmental clues
• reputation
• reports or rumors
• enemy behavior
• obvious power displays
• signs of previous victims or combat

When a threat significantly exceeds the player's current capability, provide plausible alternatives such as:
• avoiding the encounter
• retreating
• escaping
• hiding
• negotiating
• surrendering
• rescuing others without defeating the threat
• calling allies
• calling emergency services
• requesting faction support
• creating a distraction
• delaying the confrontation
• finding another route

Do not force unwinnable combat without clear narrative justification and meaningful escape or survival options.

Most superhero conflicts do not need to end in death.

Valid resolutions include:
• nonlethal defeat
• surrender
• capture
• unconsciousness
• restraint
• retreat
• escape
• negotiation
• rescue
• intervention by allies
• temporary stalemate

Enemies should behave according to their goals.

Not every enemy wants to kill the player.

Criminals may flee.
Heroes may restrain.
Vigilantes may incapacitate.
Factions may capture.
Rivals may stop once they prove a point.
Terrified opponents may surrender.
Mercenaries may withdraw when the job becomes too costly.

Lethal intent should be reserved for enemies, factions, or situations where it is established and appropriate.

Encounter difficulty should create tension without routinely overwhelming the player.

Random encounters should generally be less dangerous than:
• major quest encounters
• authored Hideout minibosses
• authored bosses
• arc villains
• major faction confrontations
• deliberately entered high-risk areas

Do not silently increase enemy numbers, durability, damage, or power complexity simply because the player is winning.

Escalation should come from established circumstances, reinforcements, enemy tactics, objectives, environmental pressure, or clearly telegraphed story stakes.
generateEncounters.Encounter Rules:
## Encounter Rules

Encounters must be meaningful, contextual, and usually optional. Most travel and everyday activity should occur without interruption.

Generate encounters only when supported by location, quests, faction activity, NPC relationships, time of day, recent actions, ongoing events, or established threats. Encounters may be combat, social scenes, investigations, rescues, arguments, strange events, rumors, NPC meetings, environmental situations, or opportunities.

When optional, allow the player to engage, observe, avoid, leave, or delay. Mandatory encounters should occur only for quests, authored events, active pursuit, established danger, justified faction interception, or situations where avoidance is implausible.

## Travel

Travel should normally:
• begin from the current location
• briefly describe route, transit, weather, crowds, traffic, or atmosphere
• arrive at the destination

Do not generate an encounter during every trip.

Routine travel to school, home, shops, dates, work, restaurants, training, social locations, and Guide Me There should usually be uninterrupted.

Do not interrupt routine travel with random combat, unrelated quests, unexplained confrontations, unjustified faction attacks, or supernatural events with no setup.

Random travel encounters should be uncommon and justified. Avoid repeating the same encounter type on consecutive trips.

Guide Me There starts normal travel and never teleports.

## Frequency

Major random encounters should be rare unless driven by quests, authored content, faction hostility, established danger, player choices, active pursuit, or major world events.

Do not use encounters as filler. Quiet travel and uneventful daily life are valid outcomes.

## Pacing

Favor low-threat, avoidable, or manageable encounters unless the current quest, authored event, Hideout, major faction conflict, or established threat requires more danger.

Scale pressure using the player's actual state:
• level
• health and injuries
• resources
• allies and party size
• attributes and skills
• power control
• equipment
• preparation
• environment
• exhaustion or status effects
• character-specific limitations

Do not scale by level alone.

Telegraph serious threats through warnings, destruction, dangerous territory, rumors, reputation, enemy behavior, power displays, or environmental clues.

If a threat greatly exceeds the player's capability, provide plausible options such as avoidance, retreat, escape, hiding, negotiation, surrender, rescue, calling allies, distraction, delay, or another route.

Do not force unwinnable combat without clear justification and meaningful survival options.

Most conflicts may end in nonlethal defeat, surrender, capture, unconsciousness, restraint, retreat, escape, negotiation, rescue, intervention, or stalemate.

Enemies act according to their goals. Not every enemy wants to kill the player.

Do not secretly increase enemy numbers, durability, damage, or power complexity because the player is winning. Escalation must come from established tactics, reinforcements, objectives, environment, or story stakes.

## NPC Knowledge Firewall

NPCs may act only on information they personally know, observed, were told, discovered, or can reasonably infer.

They must not automatically know hidden player information, private conversations, secret identities, undisclosed abilities, unseen events, information known only by other NPCs, private relationship details, or unobserved intentions.

NPCs may not appear during travel merely because they are relevant. They need a believable reason to be present or involved.

Preserve NPC schedules, locations, routines, relationships, knowledge, and current goals.

## Continuity

Respect established locations, factions, relationships, threats, quests, NPC routines, and ongoing conflicts.

Do not invent unrelated enemies, factions, organizations, or supernatural phenomena just to create an encounter.

NPCs may remember fights, favors, insults, rescues, failures, promises, public incidents, and previous meetings.

## Slice-of-Life Protection

Do not repeatedly interrupt dates, meals, shopping, classes, work, relaxation, personal conversations, training, nightlife, social events, or errands with random danger.

These scenes may remain peaceful. If tension appears, prefer social or environmental events before combat.

Sometimes nothing happens. That is intentional.

## Relevance Check

Before generating an encounter, confirm:
1. Why is this happening?
2. Why here and now?
3. Why are these NPCs or factions involved?
4. Does it connect to established world information?
5. Can the player reasonably avoid it?
6. Has something similar happened recently?

If there is no strong answer, do not generate the encounter.
generateEncounters.Procedural LFG Hideouts:
### Procedural LFG Hideouts Only

These rules apply ONLY when the player chooses:

LFG → Find Hideout Group

They do not apply to authored Hideouts.

Open LFG displays only:
Find Hideout Group

Suppress unrelated systems including:
• Starter Kit
• Gacha Wheel
• Armory
• Shops
• Inventory management
• Character rewards
• Tutorials
• unrelated menus or progression systems

## Matchmaking

Find Hideout Group immediately creates a party of exactly five participating characters including the player.

Preserve all current participating characters.

Fill only open party slots.

Never:
• wait in a matchmaking queue
• remove an existing participant
• exceed five participants
• reject matchmaking because of level differences

After exactly five participants are established:

1. Calculate party average level.
2. Use average level only for encounter pressure, miniboss strength, and loot quality.
3. Generate a NEW procedural Hideout.
4. Store the generated Hideout.
5. Create its quest.
6. Immediately accept the quest.

All of this occurs before travel begins.

Guide Me There begins normal world travel.

Guide Me There never teleports the party.

## Procedural Hideout Structure

Every standard procedural LFG Hideout contains exactly three sections:

Section 1
→ escalating combat

Section 2
→ harder combat

Section 3
→ mandatory Miniboss

Then:

Mandatory Miniboss defeated
→ guaranteed concrete Miniboss Gacha Loot
→ Extraction
→ XP reward
→ Yen reward
→ completion reward
→ Quest Complete

Standard procedural LFG Hideouts do NOT contain a Boss.

Do not add a Boss after the Miniboss.

Do not replace the Miniboss with ordinary enemies.
generateEncounters.Authored Hideouts:
### Authored Hideouts

These rules apply ONLY to Hideouts that are:

• authored by the player
• directly selected
• targeted by a quest
• otherwise explicitly established as authored content

They do NOT use Procedural LFG structure.

An Authored Hideout is a fast-paced compact mission contained within exactly ONE authored area.

Preserve:
• the authored area
• its description
• its artwork
• its atmosphere
• its party rules
• its level rules
• its loot rules
• its completion conditions
• its established enemies and objectives

Do not generate additional rooms, floors, corridors, tunnels, chambers, or traversal areas unless explicitly authored.

Resolve the Hideout directly inside the same area in this order:

Entry
→ brief Exploration
→ Encounters
→ Hazards/Objectives
→ Optional Branches
→ Exploration Loot
→ Recovery/Decision
→ mandatory Miniboss
→ Further Exploration
→ mandatory Boss OR Authored Conclusion
→ Extraction

Each step represents a meaningful gameplay beat, not a required physical room.

Present the next meaningful beat directly.

Do not require filler traversal such as:
• walking through repeated rooms
• searching for hidden hatches
• checking identical doors
• wandering corridors
• repeatedly asking where to go
• artificial navigation puzzles

Optional Branches are short choices within the same area.

Optional Branches are never required for progression.

When Hideout rules specify a Miniboss, reserve and spawn that exact Miniboss.

When Hideout rules specify a Boss, reserve and spawn that exact Boss.

Ordinary enemies may never replace a required Miniboss or Boss.

A mandatory Boss may only be omitted when the authored Hideout explicitly defines another Authored Conclusion.

ItemGenerationAndUsage.Artisan Items:
## Artisan Items
A beat that opens with ARTISAN comes from the Artisan crafting system and is an exact order for the inventory, and it is the award itself, never a second one. When it says to remove and add items, remove exactly those and add exactly the named item with exactly the category, slot and bonuses it lists. Never add an Artisan item, or a higher-quality copy of one, without such a beat. Artisan quality is a word at the front of the name: Fine, Superior, Masterwork, Legendary; an upgraded item replaces the lower one, so remove the old copy. A theme (frost, fire, venom and the like) is flavour whose effects follow this world's own rules. These rules cover only Artisan items; every other item follows this world's own item rules.

generateLearnedAbilities.Created Techniques:
## Created Techniques
A player may create a technique of their own by declaring it ("I create an ability", "my own move") and saying what it does. Honour a deliberate creation: write it under the name they gave it, in the school they placed it, at the tier their unlocks set. The tier is the school level: Tier 1 from 3, Tier 2 from 7, Tier 3 from 12, Tier 4 from 18, Tier 5 from 24, and a school below 3 creates nothing. The effect can do no more than that tier's ladder rung permits (Tier 1 a clean edge on an ordinary action, Tier 2 an advantage the raw skill only sometimes gets, Tier 3 a thing the raw skill cannot do, Tier 4 a thing that changes the fight around the character, Tier 5 the school's limit); if the character holds a core, the technique carries that core's theme. Write it like an authored technique: one flowing description that ends in its plain-language effect, a cost line ("Costs N Combat Energy." with N from 0 to 3, higher tier higher cost), and the tail [Skill: <school> <level>] [Tier N, created]. Refuse a creation that reaches past its tier, that copies an authored ability or rung, or that is a fighting technique placed in no school. These rules cover the six disciplines only: a creation that expresses a power, magic or other system the world itself defines follows the world's own rules and is never refused or tiered here. When nothing was deliberately created, prefer the ladder: if a rung, rank or core line fits what the character just did, offer that authored ability by name instead of inventing one.
Upgrading a created technique: when the player raises a technique they made, write a new ability named after it with the next rank (Iron Wind II, then Iron Wind III, and no rank past III, as with the authored techniques) whose description opens "Replaces Iron Wind." and carries the same tails; its tier is the tier the character now holds in that school (from the base's [Skill: <school> N] tail) and must be above the rank it replaces, else refuse and let the scene be refinement. An authored technique's ranks are the authored ones; never invent a rank for an ability the mod wrote.
Creating a combo together: when the player creates a technique with a named ally who is present and takes part, write it as a combo: open with "Combo with a named ally:", say what the creator does and what the ally does or gets, record it for the creator at the creator's tier. The ally gets their own half only by creating it themselves. A created combo may be upgraded like any created technique.
Fusion techniques: when the player joins two elements or states in one move of their own (lightning and water in a single strike), write it as a created technique whose description opens "Fusion of <first> and <second>:", says that it lays BOTH states on the target in one move and, when the two are a synergy pair of the Move Synergy section, that their synergy resolves at once; its tail is [Tier N, created, fusion] and its cost line is one Combat Energy more than a plain technique of its tier (at most 4). Its effect is scaled by the tier the character holds in the discipline it was made in: Tier 1 both states land but the second faint and only for this turn, no extra impact; Tier 2 both in full and a synergy pair gains one step of success; Tier 3 both in full and a synergy pair resolves its full synergy at once; Tier 4 the full synergy and both states last a round longer or spill to one adjacent enemy; Tier 5 the school's limit, the heaviest band and double Ultimate Charge. Two forces that cancel (water and fire, cold and fire, wind and gas) make no fusion: refuse it. A fusion upgrades like any created technique and keeps its [fusion] tail.
generateLearnedAbilities.Invented Skills:
## Invented Skills
When a player sets out to learn a skill this world does not have ("I teach myself lockpicking", "I study cartography" where no such skill exists) and the scene is a real lesson, book or practice, record it as an invented skill: an ability named exactly as they named the skill, whose description says what the skill covers and what it does not, ends "Not an engine skill: it never gates an authored ability and raises no check; apply it as a plain edge in the scenes it covers.", and carries the tail [Invented skill, level 1]. It costs no Combat Energy and has no cost line. Raise it the way created techniques rank up: a later study, lesson or practice scene for the same skill records a new ability named with the next rank (Lockpicking II, then Lockpicking III) whose description opens "Replaces Lockpicking." and carries [Invented skill, level N]; at most one rank per such scene, never two scenes in a short span, and never past III. Refuse to invent a skill the world already has under any name (then it is that skill, and the study trigger raises it), a skill that is really one of the six disciplines, or one invented in the middle of a fight.
generateLearnedAbilities.Created Ultimates:
## Created Ultimates
No character has an ultimate by default. Anyone who uses Awaken Ultimate (or plainly sets out to create their own ultimate) may create ONE, at any level: write it under the name they gave it, in the discipline they placed it. First look at the abilities this character holds: if one carries the tail [Tier N, created ultimate], write nothing new; a created ultimate grows only by upgrading it. A core's own ultimate is separate and does not count. Its scale is set by the character's level in that discipline and nothing else: Untiered (below 3) one target and one action, strongly improved; Tier 1 (3) one target, strongly improved, and it cannot be countered or dodged; Tier 2 (7) one target, and it also lays a state or breaks Guard; Tier 3 (12) every enemy in reach, or one effect on the character that lasts the scene; Tier 4 (18) the whole fight: every enemy in the scene, or the whole party, for the scene; Tier 5 (24) the school's limit, the scale of a core's own ultimate. Write it like an authored ultimate: the description opens "You spend the whole meter", says what it does in the character's own terms, ends in its plain-language effect, then one sentence that begins "Aftermath: " and costs the character something real in proportion to the scale (a turn with no Guard, no movement, burnout, a serious wound). It has NO Combat Energy cost line. Tail: [Skill: <school> <level>] [Tier N, created ultimate], with Tier 0 for Untiered. If the character holds a core, it carries the core's theme. One that joins two elements lays both states, with their synergy from Tier 3. Refuse one that reaches past its scale, that copies an authored ultimate, or that is a second created ultimate. It upgrades like a created technique (II, then III, at the tier the character now holds and above the rank it replaces, opening "Replaces <name>."), keeping the meter, the Aftermath and the tail.
generateLearnedAbilities.No Progress Abilities:
## No Progress Abilities
Every ability this task writes (a created technique, combo, fusion, ultimate, upgrade rank or invented skill, and a creation under the world's own power or magic rules too) acts inside a scene and nowhere else. None may grant, multiply, speed up or steal experience, levels, skill levels, attribute or stat points, ability points, a trait, another ability, currency or items that are kept, or a companion, familiar or summon that stays past the scene; none may make a training, study, rest or level-up count twice, or raise any number for good (a stat, the maximum of health or of any meter, another ability's cost or cooldown). A boost or transformation, a raised maximum included, lasts the scene at most. When a request mixes a real technique with a forbidden part ("a strike that grants XP on every kill", "a stance that permanently raises my strength"), write the technique without that part and never mention it in the description; when only the forbidden part remains, record no ability. An upgrade rank never adds such a part. The one exception is an ability the world's own rules explicitly name as granting progress.
generateLearnedAbilities.Created Abilities:
## Created Abilities
A new ability is recorded only after the player has deliberately used and TESTED the technique in play and its function, limits and cost were observable: a training-room attempt, field use, a rescue application, a controlled experiment or an improvised combat combination all qualify; discussing, naming, imagining, planning, agreeing to try later, or an NPC suggesting it do not. An NPC suggestion is dialogue and a possibility, never an unlock; the player may accept, modify, rename, combine, reject or ignore it, and only the demonstrated version is saved, never the NPC's hypothetical maximum. A failed test saves nothing: keep the partial discovery, the cost, the risk or the lesson and leave the next attempt open. A learned ability needs a plausible source (teaching, observation, experimentation, repeated practice, adapting an existing power); a mentor teaches principles, timing and risks, never the player's exact technique. Never invent the player's intent, consent, dialogue, success or emotions.
Write the ability under the name the player gave it, or a plain descriptive name if they gave none, never a name an authored ability or one of their own already carries. The description is the WHOLE mechanic, the resolver reads nothing else: one flowing paragraph that says what it does, then its stat line in plain words (see Ability Stat Block), then the tail [Lane: <power skill>] naming the power skill it resolves through (the lane of how it is expressed: Power Force for output, Power Finesse for precision, Power Endurance for sustaining, Power Theory for the mechanism, Power Control for regulation, Power Presence for will and voice; the character's Power Attribute pick breaks a tie). Bound it to what the character has shown: a first test gives a Cantrip or a Low-Level technique, never a Signature or an Ultimate.
generateLearnedAbilities.Ability Stat Block:
## Ability Stat Block
Classify every recorded ability as Attack, Defense, Healing, Mobility, Buff, Debuff, Control or Utility and give it the numbers of its band, in plain words inside the description. Bands: a Cantrip is Power 0 and No Cooldown (harmless, practice, signalling, a minor edge); a Low-Level technique is Power 5, cooldown 1 (a reliable repeatable application); a Signature is Power 10, cooldown 5 (the technique that defines the character); an Ultimate is Power 20 or more, cooldown 20, one per character, never granted automatically and only at a substantial milestone with substantial cost. A direct offensive ability is balanced against weapons, never weak by default: a clean, fully formed direct attack deals roughly 35-45, an aimed, specialised or stronger one 40-55 or higher only when justified, modified by potency, control, range, defenses, armour, hit quality, intent, Energy and Power Strain. Defense, healing, control, mobility, buff, debuff and utility resolve by their actual effect and need no damage: record magnitude, target, duration, condition and counterplay, and for a buff or debuff the one defined capability it changes. Every meaningful use has a cost: little or no Energy and negligible strain for harmless everyday use, more Energy and more Power Strain for stronger effects, and charge time, limited range, setup or a drawback for high-impact ones. A basic repeatable technique gets No Cooldown, like firing a gun or throwing a punch; cooldowns are only for unusually powerful, broad, defensive, transformative, multi-target or action-warping abilities, or an authored drawback. A fire-powered punch is a close attack with a physical component and a fire secondary effect, with burn, ignition, intimidation or area denial only where the described contact and environment support it, and a self-drawback (recoil, burns, lost control, collateral fire, extra strain) where the user lacks protection or precision; never add every possible effect. Conventional firearms carry no Energy or Power Strain cost for being fired; ammunition, reloads, condition, recoil, noise and access are their economy.
generateLearnedAbilities.Improving and Team-Ups:
## Improving and Team-Ups
Repeated meaningful use, training, experimentation or deliberate development may improve a recorded ability: more damage, stronger shielding or healing, lower Energy cost, less Power Strain, a secondary effect, broader application, or an evolved version. Record an improvement as a NEW ability named for the old one with its next step (Ember Shot, then Ember Shot II) whose description opens "Replaces Ember Shot." and carries the full stat block and the same [Lane] tail; the resolver then uses the highest version held. Improvements stay proportional to what was demonstrated, may add new restrictions, and keep the original's identity and the player's intent; a Low-Level technique becomes a Signature only through a substantial, played development, and nothing becomes an Ultimate by improvement alone.
Team-ups may be planned, practised or improvised in combat with present party members and need no prior record: resolve the attempt from each participant's actual position, capability, timing, communication, awareness, willingness, injuries, resources and objectives, each paying their own Energy and Power Strain; account for setup, exposure, range, target conditions and coordination failure, and never make an NPC participate, spend, consent or use a signature technique without a plausible reason or the player's direction. A successful improvised combination may stay a one-time tactic. Record a team-up ability only after the participants meaningfully perform and test it and the player or group chooses to keep it: write it for the player who declared it, opening "Team-up with <ally>:", saying what each participant does and pays, with its stat block and [Lane] tail; the ally records their own half only by performing it themselves.
generateLearnedAbilities.Progression Bands:
## Progression Bands

Starting ability points: 2.

Every newly created player character, regardless of story start, begins at Level 1 with 2 freely spendable starting ability points in addition to one automatic power-derived offensive Starter ability. Story starts must not remove, replace, or omit these 2 points. The Starter ability is granted directly and does not consume either starting point. Starting points may be used for additional abilities according to the Starter, Standard, Signature, and Ultimate progression bands. The Starter ability has no cooldown, costs Power Strain, and remains limited by the chosen power and the user's established constraints. Standard abilities are reliable trained applications; Signature abilities are defining techniques with stronger effects and meaningful costs; each character may develop one Ultimate with scaled power, substantial costs, strong limitations, and a long cooldown or once-per-encounter/scene restriction. Do not grant an Ultimate automatically. Abilities that cost 0 points are valid freely available foundational techniques when explicitly granted by a power, trait, NPC, quest, or authored progression; they do not consume starting ability points and should remain limited by the ability's description, resources, cooldown, range, risk, and established power constraints.
generateLearnedAbilities.Power Awakenings:
## Power Awakenings
Each Power Style has three Awakening traits (Awakened, Breakthrough, Pinnacle), taken as level-up trait picks at levels 10, 20 and 30, each granting its own technique. Never generate a learned ability that duplicates or pre-empts the next Awakening technique of the character's style; a created ability may build on an Awakening technique the character already holds, as an improvement named "<X> II" whose description opens "Replaces <X>.". An Awakening technique rolls the character's power lane like every power check (Power Routing).

generateAbilities.custom: Not a Voyage task: see generateLearnedAbilities (Created Abilities, Ability Stat Block, Improving and Team-Ups).

Chikara Tokyo.name: Chikara Tokyo
Chikara Tokyo.basicInfo: A unified Tokyo realm for Chikara Academy's superhero-anime world, connecting academy life, colorful districts, hero agencies, ordinary neighborhoods, criminal networks, apartments, workplaces, and waterfront operations.

Chikara Tokyo.name: Chikara Tokyo
Chikara Tokyo.basicInfo: The unified Tokyo region containing Chikara Academy, student neighborhoods, hero institutions, everyday businesses, criminal routes, apartments, and waterfront operations.
Chikara Tokyo.hiddenInfo: Walking and rail travel connect the city. Flight, swinging, portals, and teleportation provide alternate routes only when the character's abilities, range, anchors, and access permit them.

Chikara Academy.name: Chikara Academy
Chikara Academy.basicInfo: A prestigious superhero university in Tokyo combining rigorous academics, power training, rescue simulations, student life, supervised hero development, and coed dormitory living.

campus-footbridge.description: Raised pedestrian bridge connecting the academy to surrounding campus paths, with city lights and passing trains below. Suitable for brief meetings and farewells.

classroom-3c.description: Homeroom of Class 3C: rows of desks under tall windows, a scuffed lectern, and a power-control practice corner at the back where Keito Takeda runs drills between lessons.

classroom-4d.description: Homeroom of Class 4D: a warm, slightly cluttered classroom with snack boxes on the teacher's desk, student artwork on the back wall, and Kaede Arashiro's attendance sheets forever one drawer away.

classroom-5a.description: Homeroom of Class 5A: a bright upper-year classroom with lab benches along one side, a projector wall, and a quiet study nook the senior students treat as their own.

main-hall.description: Central hall with hero memorials, class rosters, schedules, Pulse kiosks, club notices, and Battle Test announcements.

north-rooftop-overlook.description: Accessible rooftop overlook with safety lighting, benches, and a wide view over Chikara District. Useful for late-night conversations, recovery, stargazing, and difficult decisions.

student-courtyard.description: Open paved courtyard between academic wings, with benches, shade trees, noticeboards, and room for casual conversations.

vending-machine-nook.description: Covered seating beside vending machines. Bright, public, and open late for casual meals, phone calls, awkward encounters, and nighttime scenes.

west-service-alley.description: Visible service alley along the academy wall for deliveries, maintenance carts, and quieter travel. It is not hidden.

Chikara Academy.hiddenInfo: A sealed sublevel beneath the academy contains records about early Ultra Force operations and may connect to the player's family history. This is hidden information and restricted access within the globally visible academy, not a hidden map location.

Old Tokyo Shrine Road.name: Old Tokyo Shrine Road
Old Tokyo Shrine Road.basicInfo: Historic shrine district with traditional restaurants, tea houses, antiques, tunnels, shops, and a preserved station.

heritage-store.description: Antique, charm, book, and traditional craft store.

lantern-restaurant.description: Traditional restaurant serving seasonal dishes near the shrine.

old-tokyo-station.description: Historic station connecting old and modern Tokyo.

tea-house.description: Restaurant and tea house for dates and negotiations.

Ultra Force Headquarters.name: Ultra Force Headquarters
Ultra Force Headquarters.basicInfo: Secure hero complex with operations, archives, training, medicine, stores, dining, communal barracks facilities, and a credentialed station. The barracks are reserved for Blacklisted recruits and provisional operatives whose story explicitly assigns them there. Everyday Zero's civilian dispatch coordinator remains based at Apartment 68; visiting Ultra Force Headquarters for work does not change the player's home or residence. Resolve "go home" using the player's established residence, not the barracks, unless a story explicitly establishes otherwise.

barracks.description: Monitored shared sleeping quarters for Blacklisted recruits and provisional operatives. These quarters are not assigned to ordinary civilian dispatch staff or Everyday Zero players. Only a story that explicitly places the player in Blacklisted recruitment or provisional housing may make the barracks their home. The random roommate shares the sleeping space, while privacy is limited and movement is logged.

command-mess.description: Hero cafeteria and restaurant for staff meals and briefings.

communal-bathroom.description: Shared barracks bathroom with communal showers, bath facilities, lockers, and strict schedules. Use only privacy-respecting, nonsexual comedy such as queue disputes, missing toiletries, plumbing problems, or harmless power accidents.

dispatch-floor.description: The dedicated Ultra Force dispatch floor: a wall of live incident boards, call consoles, response maps, agency status panels, secure phone lines, staffed routing desks, and a posted Ultra Force Dispatch Reference Guide. Dispatch coordinators assess callers, verify locations, check hero availability, route small local threats and practical paid-service cases to Hero for Hire responders, send specialized cases to the appropriate faction, escalate emergencies, and record follow-up reports. The floor includes adult civilian operations staff, pro heroes, supervised Blacklisted personnel, and coworkers; it is a workplace, not a student area.

hero-supply-store.description: Authorized store for costumes, support gear, field supplies, and recovery products.

operations-floor.description: Mission dispatch and monitoring floor where civilian calls, agency requests, police referrals, supernatural alerts, and hero availability are assessed. Dispatch staff triage each case, record details, choose an appropriate response, and route ordinary incidents to the faction or hero organization best suited to handle them.

Old Tokyo Lantern Quarter.name: Old Tokyo Lantern Quarter
Old Tokyo Lantern Quarter.basicInfo: Preserved neighborhood of lantern-lit alleys, craft workshops, seasonal food, and cultural events.

craft-row.description: Workshops selling ceramics, paper goods, charms, and crafts.

festival-court.description: Courtyard for performances, dances, and seasonal celebrations.

lantern-alley.description: Historic alley lined with lanterns, galleries, and food stalls.

seasonal-restaurant.description: Traditional dining room serving regional dishes and tea.

Old Tokyo Tea Market Street.name: Old Tokyo Tea Market Street
Old Tokyo Tea Market Street.basicInfo: Historic shopping street with groceries, tea merchants, gifts, and traditional restaurants.

grocery-stalls.description: Produce, preserved foods, spices, and ingredients.

Central Tokyo Station.name: Central Tokyo Station
Central Tokyo Station.basicInfo: Major public rail interchange with ticket counters, express platforms, route boards, and connections across Tokyo. When the player enters, a station attendant approaches to offer route and ticket help.

concourse.description: Large central concourse with maps, ticket machines, staffed counters, and departure boards. You can buy a train ticket here before boarding.

platforms.description: Platforms for Academy District, Old Tokyo, Tokyo Bay, Shadow District, and Ultra Force Headquarters. Boarding requires a valid ticket or approved access.

station-retail.description: Shops, cafés, lockers, and passenger services.

ticket-counter.description: Ticket office and automated machines. The game should tell the player they can buy a ticket here, select a destination, and pay the listed fare.

Imperial Palace East Gardens.name: Imperial Palace East Gardens
Imperial Palace East Gardens.basicInfo: Historic gardens and preserved palace grounds with stone walls, seasonal landscaping, paths, and civic landmarks.

garden-paths.description: Stone walls, lawns, seasonal trees, and historic foundations.

moat-walk.description: Scenic outer path beside water and fortified walls.

public-gate.description: Public entrance with visitor information and security guidance.

Chiyoda Civic Offices.name: Chiyoda Civic Offices
Chiyoda Civic Offices.basicInfo: Municipal offices handling permits, records, public services, neighborhood administration, and civic complaints.

public-counter.description: Public service counters for forms, permits, and resident questions.

waiting-hall.description: Seating and information boards for visitors.

Marunouchi Business Avenue.name: Marunouchi Business Avenue
Marunouchi Business Avenue.basicInfo: A polished office corridor of corporate towers, underground passages, restaurants, hotels, and weekday commuter traffic.

avenue.description: Wide office avenue with plazas, taxis, and business crowds.

tower-lobby.description: Corporate reception areas and visitor security desks.

underground-mall.description: Restaurants, cafés, shops, and connected pedestrian passages.

Tokyo Skytree Tower Complex.name: Tokyo Skytree Tower Complex
Tokyo Skytree Tower Complex.basicInfo: A landmark tower and commercial complex with observation decks, shops, restaurants, and broad views across Tokyo.

observation-deck.description: High viewing decks above the city.

tower-plaza.description: Public plaza beneath the tower with shops and event spaces.

Nakano Residential Arcade.name: Nakano Residential Arcade
Nakano Residential Arcade.basicInfo: A neighborhood shopping arcade serving apartment residents with groceries, bakeries, clinics, laundries, and family restaurants.

grocery-row.description: Markets, bakeries, pharmacies, and daily services.

Gearshift Support.name: Gearshift Support
Gearshift Support.basicInfo: Compact support-technology workshop where students help repair approved hero equipment, sort parts, and assist customers.

parts-counter.description: Components, diagnostic tools, and customer intake.

staff-office.description: Schedules, job records, and safety approvals.

workshop-floor.description: Repair benches and supervised prototype stations.

Page Turner Books.name: Page Turner Books
Page Turner Books.basicInfo: Independent bookstore with study tables, hero biographies, and a quiet inventory room.

stockroom.description: Inventory shelves and staff work area. A curious viper fang pendant rests in a forgotten storage crate.

Game Start Arcade.name: Game Start Arcade
Game Start Arcade.basicInfo: Colorful student arcade with competitive games, prize machines, after-school shifts, and a lively social scene.

arcade-floor.description: Cabinets, rhythm games, and prize machines.

prize-counter.description: Prize redemption and customer service desk.

staff-room.description: Break area, supplies, and shift board.

Crepe Expectations.name: Crepe Expectations
Crepe Expectations.basicInfo: Friendly crepe café with a compact kitchen, counter service, and student shifts.

Rescue Volunteer Desk.name: Rescue Volunteer Desk
Rescue Volunteer Desk.basicInfo: Public service desk connecting volunteers with approved welfare checks, visitor assistance, and community support.

help-desk.description: Reception for requests, directions, and volunteer intake.

quiet-room.description: Calm waiting room for visitors needing support.

records-room.description: Schedules, supplies, and supervised case files.

Uniform & Co..name: Uniform & Co.
Uniform & Co..basicInfo: Academy District clothing shop selling school uniforms, casual clothes, costume alterations, and practical accessories for students.

alterations-counter.description: Tailoring desk for repairs, adjustments, and costume-safe alterations.

back-workroom.description: Staff workroom with sewing machines and fabric supplies.

fitting-rooms.description: Private fitting stalls for uniforms and casual clothing.

sales-floor.description: Uniform racks, everyday clothing, bags, and approved accessories.

Hero Hobby Shop.name: Hero Hobby Shop
Hero Hobby Shop.basicInfo: A hobby store filled with hero collectibles, model kits, training memorabilia, craft supplies, and novelty power-themed merchandise.

craft-corner.description: Tables for painting models, assembling kits, and sharing hobby advice.

display-gallery.description: Rotating displays of famous heroes, academy memorabilia, and local artists.

main-floor.description: Shelves of figures, model kits, cards, comics, and hero merchandise.

Neon Karaoke.basicInfo: A colorful karaoke venue with private rooms where students celebrate, vent, practice songs, and build friendships after dark.

karaoke-room.description: Soundproof room for singing, conversations, challenges, and group scenes.

reception.description: Front desk with room bookings, song catalogs, and time packages.

snack-bar.description: Counter serving drinks and quick food to guests.

Midnight Diner.name: Midnight Diner
Midnight Diner.basicInfo: An all-night American-style diner in Chikara Tokyo, serving affordable comfort food twenty-four hours a day to students, workers, travelers, night-shift staff, and anyone who needs a booth and a quiet place to talk. The menu combines familiar American diner staples with a few practical Tokyo touches.

booths.description: Rows of private red-vinyl booths for families, dates, students, tired workers, and late-night conversations.

counter.description: Long counter with swivel stools, a coffee station, napkin holders, condiment caddies, and a view of the open kitchen. Regulars and night-shift workers often sit here.

dining-room.description: Warm all-night dining room with red vinyl booths, chrome-edged tables, counter seats, laminated menus, pie display, coffee refills, and large front windows showing the street outside.

kitchen.description: Open diner kitchen preparing burgers, cheeseburgers, fries, pancakes, waffles, eggs, bacon, grilled cheese, chicken sandwiches, milkshakes, coffee, pie, and rotating specials. A few rice bowls or other Tokyo-friendly options are available without changing the restaurant's American-diner identity.

Pulse Printworks.name: Pulse Printworks
Pulse Printworks.basicInfo: A small print and copy shop producing flyers, posters, club materials, event banners, and local campaign notices for the academy district.

design-booth.description: Computer station for layouts, posters, club flyers, and campaign materials.

front-counter.description: Order desk for printing, copying, binding, and design requests.

print-floor.description: Printers, cutters, binding machines, paper stock, and finished orders.

supply-room.description: Paper, ink, packaging, and staff storage.

Power Practice Studio.name: Power Practice Studio
Power Practice Studio.basicInfo: A supervised neighborhood studio offering safe power-control lessons, civilian exercises, and beginner sessions for students and residents.

equipment-room.description: Storage for protective gear, targets, and calibration tools.

observation-room.description: Viewing area for guardians, instructors, and controlled demonstrations.

practice-floor.description: Padded training space with adjustable barriers and safety monitors.

reception.description: Booking desk with lesson schedules, waivers, and instructor information.

Student Clinic.name: Student Clinic
Student Clinic.basicInfo: A walk-in neighborhood clinic serving academy students, residents, and workers with routine care, minor injuries, and referrals.

exam-room.description: Private room for routine examinations and minor injuries.

pharmacy-window.description: Dispensing window for approved prescriptions and care instructions.

reception.description: Check-in desk, seating, appointment board, and intake forms.

treatment-room.description: Treatment space for first aid, observation, and power-related precautions.

Riverside Food Market.name: Riverside Food Market
Riverside Food Market.basicInfo: A lively market near the river with produce stalls, prepared food, household basics, and inexpensive groceries for students and residents.

food-stalls.description: Quick meals, desserts, and rotating local vendors.

fresh-counter.description: Produce, prepared meals, and refrigerated goods.

market-exit.description: Street-facing exit beside delivery lanes and pedestrian paths.

market-hall.description: Covered market aisle with produce, pantry goods, and household supplies.

Open-Air Performance Stage.name: Open-Air Performance Stage
Open-Air Performance Stage.basicInfo: A public stage for school events, local musicians, Pulse broadcasts, festivals, speeches, and spontaneous student performances.

audience-plaza.description: Open public space with benches, food carts, and room for crowds.

backstage.description: Restricted preparation area for performers, staff, and equipment.

park-walkway.description: Path connecting the stage to nearby park and market routes.

stage.description: Raised performance platform with lighting, sound equipment, and event access.

Tokyo Tower.name: Tokyo Tower
Tokyo Tower.basicInfo: Iconic red communications tower and Central Tokyo landmark with observation decks, public event spaces, broadcast infrastructure, and a commanding view over the city.

broadcast-level.description: Communications equipment and broadcast infrastructure hidden above the public spaces.

main-observation-deck.description: Panoramic observation deck overlooking Tokyo and the surrounding districts.

observation-lobby.description: Visitor lobby and elevator access for the public observation decks.

service-access.description: Restricted maintenance and broadcast access used by authorized staff and emergency crews.

tower-foot.description: Landmark plaza with visitors, food stands, ticket booths, and public gatherings.

upper-deck.description: Higher observation level with exhibits, dramatic views, and special-event access.

Hero Agency Row.name: Hero Agency Row
Hero Agency Row.basicInfo: A Central Tokyo avenue lined with professional hero agencies, licensing offices, public relations firms, and internship opportunities.

agency-cafe.description: Café where assistants, interns, reporters, and heroes meet between appointments.

agency-street.description: Busy avenue of agency entrances, hero billboards, and professional support services.

public-relations-office.description: Media coordination and reputation-management offices serving hero agencies.

reception-lobby.description: Shared lobby for agency appointments, deliveries, and internship inquiries.

Pulse Media Tower.name: Pulse Media Tower
Pulse Media Tower.basicInfo: Central Tokyo broadcasting and news tower where hero coverage, interviews, public statements, and Fame-shaping stories are produced.

broadcast-lobby.description: Public lobby with news screens, visitor passes, and rotating hero coverage.

newsroom.description: Editors and reporters track incidents, academy news, hero performances, and public reaction. An old props drawer holds a plain metal band inscribed with unfamiliar letters.

press-room.description: Press briefing room for agency statements and major public events.

studio-floor.description: Television and streaming studios for interviews, debates, announcements, and live segments.

Tokyo Hero Plaza.name: Tokyo Hero Plaza
Tokyo Hero Plaza.basicInfo: A large public square honoring professional heroes through memorials, statues, event stages, demonstrations, and civic gatherings.

event-square.description: Open plaza for ceremonies, festivals, demonstrations, protests, and public hero appearances.

food-kiosks.description: Public food stalls and souvenir stands serving visitors and office workers.

hero-gallery.description: Indoor exhibit space displaying equipment, records, and licensed hero history.

memorial-walk.description: Path of hero statues, plaques, memorials, and historical displays.

Professional Hero Hospital.name: Professional Hero Hospital
Professional Hero Hospital.basicInfo: Specialized Central Tokyo hospital treating professional heroes, power-related injuries, emergency responders, and civilians affected by incidents.

emergency-entrance.description: Protected emergency intake for urgent injuries and incident victims.

outpatient-wing.description: Clinics for follow-up care, rehabilitation, and power-related assessments.

reception.description: Main desk handling appointments, visitors, records, and referrals.

rehabilitation-gym.description: Supervised recovery space for mobility, conditioning, and safe power rehabilitation.

trauma-ward.description: Secure treatment area for serious injuries and emergency observation.

visitor-lounge.description: Waiting area for families, agency staff, students, and authorized visitors.

Hero Licensing Bureau.name: Hero Licensing Bureau
Hero Licensing Bureau.basicInfo: Official Central Tokyo office handling hero licenses, permits, examinations, records, and regulated professional activity.

examination-wing.description: Testing rooms for written, practical, and renewal examinations.

public-lobby.description: Reception, information screens, forms, and visitor guidance.

records-counter.description: Secure counter for licenses, permits, identity checks, and official records.

staff-office.description: Restricted offices where examiners and administrators review applications.

Tokyo Metropolitan Government Office.name: Tokyo Metropolitan Government Office
Tokyo Metropolitan Government Office.basicInfo: Major civic office complex where public policy, emergency coordination, permits, city planning, and official hero oversight are handled.

council-wing.description: Meeting rooms and offices for metropolitan policy and public hearings.

emergency-coordination.description: Operations room coordinating city services during major incidents.

public-hall.description: Public service counters, notices, visitor screening, and city information.

restricted-briefing.description: Secure briefing room for authorized emergency and hero officials.

Executive Dining Tower.name: Executive Dining Tower
Executive Dining Tower.basicInfo: Upscale Central Tokyo dining venue where agency leaders, executives, officials, and ambitious professionals hold private meals and negotiations.

lobby.description: Elegant reception with reservations, security, and skyline elevators.

main-dining-room.description: High-end restaurant floor for formal meals and public networking.

private-suites.description: Reserved rooms for confidential meetings, negotiations, and celebrations.

skyline-terrace.description: Outdoor terrace with a sweeping view of Central Tokyo.

Hero Equipment Exchange.name: Hero Equipment Exchange
Hero Equipment Exchange.basicInfo: Licensed Central Tokyo marketplace for approved support gear, refurbished equipment, protective clothing, and regulated trade-ins.

fitting-bay.description: Supervised testing area for checking fit, mobility, and basic function.

secured-storage.description: Restricted storage for regulated equipment and high-value orders.

service-counter.description: Appraisals, repairs, trade-ins, and purchase paperwork.

showroom.description: Displays of approved support tools, protective equipment, and refurbished gear.

Metropolitan Police Headquarters.name: Metropolitan Police Headquarters
Metropolitan Police Headquarters.basicInfo: Major police headquarters coordinating investigations, emergency response, public safety, and official cooperation with licensed heroes. The building includes public services, secure investigative spaces, command operations, training facilities, and staff areas that support officers through long shifts.

evidence-room.description: Restricted evidence storage and forensic intake.

investigations-wing.description: Case offices and interview rooms for authorized investigations.

locker-room.description: Officer lockers, changing benches, equipment checklists, and secure preparation space before or after a shift.

operations-center.description: Command floor coordinating citywide incidents and emergency response.

police-gym.description: A practical headquarters gym with mats, free weights, punching bags, cardio machines, and a small defensive-training area. Officers may work out, practice restraint techniques, recover after shifts, or observe one another's routines. Training is voluntary and does not assume the player participates.

public-entrance.description: Visitor screening, public information, and report guidance.

secure-briefing.description: Controlled room for police, officials, and licensed hero briefings.

staff-cafeteria.description: A bright, functional cafeteria serving shift meals, coffee, vending-machine snacks, and informal conversation between officers, dispatchers, investigators, and support staff.

Metropolitan Police Headquarters.hiddenInfo: The headquarters gym is available to officers but is not a mandatory conditioning program. Early mornings are quieter, while shift changes make the cafeteria and locker room busier. Hana reliably works out in the police gym early each morning when duty, injury, or an active emergency does not prevent it; she focuses on disciplined strength, cardio, firearms posture, and close-quarters fundamentals. She does not automatically invite the player, and the player is never required to join.

Tokyo Tower 7-Eleven.name: Tokyo Tower 7-Eleven
Tokyo Tower 7-Eleven.basicInfo: Tourist-heavy convenience store at Tokyo Tower's base, selling snacks, drinks, souvenirs, camera supplies, and essentials for visitors.

checkout.description: Register with souvenir displays and visitor service.

storage-room.description: Compact employee storage and delivery access.

store-floor.description: Tourist shelves of snacks, drinks, souvenirs, and travel essentials.

Tokyo Business Hotel.name: Tokyo Business Hotel
Tokyo Business Hotel.basicInfo: Professional hotel in Central Tokyo where agency staff, visiting officials, reporters, and out-of-town heroes stay between meetings and assignments.

conference-floor.description: Meeting rooms and small event spaces for business functions.

executive-lounge.description: Private lounge for professionals and quiet networking.

guest-floors.description: Comfortable private rooms and corridors for lodgers.

hotel-room.description: Well-appointed room for resting, preparing, and private calls.

lobby.description: Reception, business desks, lounges, and conference access.

Tokyo Underground Mall.name: Tokyo Underground Mall
Tokyo Underground Mall.basicInfo: Extensive below-street shopping mall with clothing shops, food stalls, boutiques, bookstores, and commuter routes beneath Central Tokyo.

central-carrefour.description: Busy underground junction of shops, signage, and commuter flows.

food-wing.description: Food stalls, bakeries, cafés, and quick meals.

transit-connection.description: Corridor linking the mall to station platforms and city streets.

Central Tokyo Taxi Stand.name: Central Tokyo Taxi Stand
Central Tokyo Taxi Stand.basicInfo: Local taxi stand with licensed drivers serving Central Tokyo destinations, offering convenient city transport and opportunity for roadside encounters.

curbside.description: Pickup and drop-off point beside the station and street.

dispatch-hut.description: Small office coordinating rides, fares, and local routes.

taxi-rank.description: Queue of parked taxis with dispatchers and waiting drivers.

Traditional Bathhouse.name: Traditional Bathhouse
Traditional Bathhouse.basicInfo: Neighborhood sento in a preserved wooden building where residents, travelers, and visitors unwind, exchange rumors, and observe local customs.

bathing-hall.description: Traditional bathing area with tiled pools, washing stations, and steam.

changing-room.description: Separate changing areas leading to the bathing halls.

entrance-lobby.description: Reception with shoe lockers, towels, refreshments, and a small waiting area.

resting-room.description: Quiet lounge with tea, milk drinks, fans, and neighborhood conversation.

Riverside Lantern Promenade.name: Riverside Lantern Promenade
Riverside Lantern Promenade.basicInfo: Historic riverside walking route lined with lanterns, stone railings, seasonal stalls, and views of Old Tokyo's traditional neighborhoods.

lantern-walk.description: Long riverside path for evening walks, dates, festivals, and quiet reflection.

river-overlook.description: Stone overlook with benches and a broad view of the river.

riverside-entrance.description: Street entrance leading down toward the lantern-lined waterfront.

seasonal-stalls.description: Rotating stalls serving tea, sweets, crafts, and festival food.

Heritage Theater.name: Heritage Theater
Heritage Theater.basicInfo: Traditional performance venue for kabuki-inspired drama, music, dance, puppet theater, cultural festivals, and visiting performers.

auditorium.description: Main theater with traditional stage machinery and audience seating.

backstage.description: Restricted dressing rooms, props, rehearsal space, and performer access.

rehearsal-room.description: Practice room for actors, musicians, dancers, and puppeteers.

ticket-hall.description: Ticket desk and foyer decorated with posters, programs, and historic costumes.

Ultra Force Station.name: Ultra Force Station
Ultra Force Station.basicInfo: Secure transit station serving Ultra Force Headquarters, authorized personnel, and approved visitors traveling across Tokyo.

concourse.description: Credential checkpoint, route boards, ticket services, and controlled visitor access.

platforms.description: Secure platforms connecting to Central Tokyo and authorized city routes.

security-desk.description: Identity checks, visitor passes, and transit clearance.

ticket-counter.description: Station desk for approved fares, travel authorization, and route information.

Ultra Force Training Annex.name: Ultra Force Training Annex
Ultra Force Training Annex.basicInfo: Compact secured training facility for tactical drills, rescue simulations, power control, and supervised hero evaluations.

check-in.description: Credentialed entrance with schedules, equipment issue, and instructor assignments.

observation-deck.description: Instructor and evaluator viewing area overlooking active drills.

power-control-room.description: Monitored room for testing output, precision, collateral control, and safe limits.

simulation-floor.description: Reconfigurable space for rescue, pursuit, combat, and team exercises.

Ultra Force Memorial Plaza.name: Ultra Force Memorial Plaza
Ultra Force Memorial Plaza.basicInfo: Formal memorial square honoring Ultra Force heroes, fallen responders, historic missions, and public service.

central-monument.description: Main memorial used for ceremonies, speeches, and commemorations.

ceremony-steps.description: Open steps for official events, public addresses, and wreath-laying ceremonies.

memorial-walk.description: Stone path with plaques, statues, names, and mission histories.

reflection-garden.description: Quiet landscaped garden for private remembrance and conversations.

Ultra Force Medical Wing.name: Ultra Force Medical Wing
Ultra Force Medical Wing.basicInfo: Specialized medical facility for Ultra Force personnel, power-related injuries, emergency recovery, and confidential rehabilitation.

consultation-room.description: Private room for medical briefings, referrals, and confidential care plans.

intake.description: Secure intake for authorized patients and urgent field injuries.

rehabilitation-room.description: Controlled recovery space for mobility, conditioning, and monitored power use.

treatment-bay.description: Medical treatment area for trauma, power strain, and emergency stabilization.

Ultra Force Visitor Center.name: Ultra Force Visitor Center

credential-desk.description: Desk for visitor passes, appointment verification, and access instructions.

public-lobby.description: Reception, visitor screening, public notices, and check-in for approved guests.

tour-gallery.description: Controlled exhibit space showing Ultra Force history, equipment, and public-service missions.

visitor-cafe.description: Small café serving visitors, staff, and approved guests during tours or meetings.

Ultra Force Recreation Lounge.name: Ultra Force Recreation Lounge
Ultra Force Recreation Lounge.basicInfo: Secure staff recreation space where Ultra Force personnel rest, socialize, play games, and decompress between missions and training.

fitness-corner.description: Compact exercise area for stretching, conditioning, and recovery routines.

media-room.description: Screens, consoles, and mission broadcasts for supervised downtime.

quiet-room.description: Low-stimulation room for reading, reflection, and private conversations.

Ultra Force Supply Depot.name: Ultra Force Supply Depot
Ultra Force Supply Depot.basicInfo: Restricted logistics facility storing uniforms, approved support gear, medical supplies, emergency equipment, and mission consumables.

administration-office.description: Requisition desk for authorization, inventory records, and deployment paperwork.

equipment-floor.description: Organized storage for uniforms, field kits, protective equipment, and supplies.

intake-bay.description: Loading area where deliveries, returns, and mission requisitions are processed.

secured-vault.description: Restricted storage for regulated equipment and high-value emergency stock.

Ultra Force Communications Center.name: Ultra Force Communications Center
Ultra Force Communications Center.basicInfo: Secure communications facility coordinating mission dispatch, emergency alerts, field reports, encrypted messages, and citywide response networks.

briefing-booth.description: Small rooms for field reports, interviews, and mission debriefs.

dispatch-floor.description: Operators assign missions, monitor incidents, and coordinate authorized responders.

secure-comms.description: Encrypted communications room for sensitive messages and command traffic.

Bay Lantern.name: Bay Lantern
Bay Lantern.basicInfo: Popular waterfront restaurant serving fresh bay seafood, grilled dishes, seasonal specials, and harbor-view meals.

counter-bar.description: Informal counter serving daily seafood specials and chef recommendations.

dining-room.description: Main seating area for casual meals, dates, celebrations, and harbor conversations.

Oblivion's Crucible.hiddenInfo: The Crucible is a dangerous, optional underworld venue. Jobs, matches, recruitment offers, drinks, rumors, and introductions may be useful, deceptive, exploitative, or traps. Do not force a character to fight, drink, join a faction, accept a contract, or obey Oblivion. Preserve existing story references to oblivion-box and arena-floor while using the clearly named areas for new scenes. Fights in the fighting-ring and arena-floor must use context-appropriate opponents: powered villains, unlicensed vigilantes, mercenaries, criminal fighters, dangerous contractors, cursed or supernatural combatants, or other explicitly authored participants connected to the Crucible. Do not generate old office workers, elderly civilians, generic office employees, random civilian workers, or unrelated ordinary NPCs as fighters or combat opponents. Ordinary civilians may appear only as spectators, staff, bettors, medical personnel, or bystanders when appropriate, never as default combatants.
